Kaggle Cars Dataset Exploration¶

Preliminary Wrangling¶

This document explores a dataset containing car brands and their engineering attributes for approximately 261 models.

Cleaning Steps:¶

  • Remove whitespaces in column names.
  • Convert cubicinches & weightlbs into integer type.
In [7]:
# Removing whitespaces in column names.
for x in list(cars.columns):
    cars = cars.rename(columns={x:x.strip()})
In [8]:
# Converting the cubicinches feature into an integer type.
cars['cubicinches'] = pd.to_numeric(cars['cubicinches'], errors='coerce')
cars['cubicinches'] =  cars['cubicinches'].ffill(axis=0)
cars['cubicinches'] = cars['cubicinches'].astype(int)
In [9]:
# Converting the weightlbs feature into an integer type.
cars['weightlbs'] = pd.to_numeric(cars['weightlbs'], errors="coerce")
cars['weightlbs'] = cars['weightlbs'].ffill(axis=0)
cars['weightlbs'] = cars['weightlbs'].astype('int64')

The structure of the dataset:¶

There are 261 car models in the dataset with 8 features: mpg, cylinders, cubicinches, hp, weightlbs, time-to-60, year and brand. Most variables are numeric in nature, except for the variable brand, which is a categorical variable and the year variable, which is a period.

The main features of interest in the dataset:¶

I'm interested in figuring out how mpg, cylinders, cubicinches, hp, weightlbs, time-to-60, year, and brand are related to one another in the dataset, specifically, how these variables change overtime.

The features in the dataset that I think will help support the investigation into the features of interest:¶

All previously mentioned features will provide great insights into how models' size, speed, force, weight, and fuel consumption have changed across time and place.

Univariate Exploration¶

In this section, we'll investigate distributions of individual variables.

1. Distribution of Miles Per Gallon¶

In [11]:
# Plotting a histogram of the mpg feature:
bin_edges = np.arange(10, 47+2.5, 2.5)
plt.hist(data=cars, x='mpg', bins=bin_edges)
plt.xlabel('MPG')
plt.ylabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By MPG');

The mpg histogram is skewed to the right. Car models with higher miles per gallon are lower in frequency. The number of car models increases, as the miles per gallon variable decreases, meaning that fewer car models achieve the highest efficiency regarding fuel consumption.

2. Distribution of Number of Cylinders¶

In [12]:
# Plotting a Pareto chart of the cylinders feature:
sns.countplot(data=cars, x='cylinders', order=[4, 8, 6, 5, 3])
plt.xlabel('Engine Cylinders')
plt.ylabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By The Number of Cylinders');

The cylinders Pareto chart shows that cars with engines of 4 cylinders are the most frequent then cars with 8 cylinders, 6 cylinders, 5, and lastly 3 cylinders.

3. Distribution of Horsepower¶

In [13]:
# Plotting a histogram of the hp feature:
bin_edges = np.arange(46, 230+13, 13)
plt.hist(data=cars, x='hp', bins=bin_edges)
plt.xlabel('Horse power')
plt.ylabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By Horse Power');

The hp histogram is skewed to the right. As horsepower increases, the frequency decreases. Most cars are ranged between 50 and 150 for horse power.

4. Distribution of Time-To-60¶

In [14]:
# Plotting a histogram of the time-to-60 feature:
bin_edges = np.arange(8, 25+1.2, 1.2)
plt.hist(data=cars, x='time-to-60', bins=bin_edges)
plt.xlabel('Time-To-60 (S)')
plt.ylabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By Time-To-60');

The time-to-60 histogram is unimodal. As for time-to-60 variable, most cars in the dataset take about 10-20 seconds to reach 60 miles per hour.

5. Distribution of Brand¶

In [15]:
# Plotting a Pareto chart of the brand feature:
sns.countplot(data=cars, x='brand', order=cars['brand'].value_counts().index)
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('Count Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By Brand');

The brand bar chart shows that most cars in our dataset are US brands then Japanese and lastly European.

6. Distribution of Year¶

In [16]:
# Plotting a Pareto chart of the year feature:
sns.countplot(data=cars, y='year', order=cars.year.value_counts().index)
plt.xlabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.ylabel('Year')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By Year');

From the year Pareto chart all the car models in the dataset were designed in the seventies and the eighties. The top five years regarding the number of models are 1974, 1977, 1971, 1976, and 1980 or 1979 given that these two years have the same count of car models.

7. Distribution of Cubicinches¶

In [17]:
# Plotting a histogram of the cubicinches feature:
bin_edges = np.arange(68, 455+25, 25)
plt.hist(data=cars, x='cubicinches', bins=bin_edges)
plt.xlabel('Cubicinches')
plt.ylabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By Cubicinches');

The cubicinches histogram is skewed to the right. The higher this feature, the lower the frequency in the data. Most cars range between 100 and 350.

8. Distribution of Weights¶

In [18]:
# Plotting a histogram of the weightslbs feature:
bin_edges = np.arange(1613, 4997+250, 250)
plt.hist(data=cars, x='weightlbs', bins=bin_edges)
plt.xlabel('Weights')
plt.ylabel('Count of Car Models')
plt.title('Frequency of Car Models By Weights');

The weightlbs histogram is skewed to the right. As cars weight increases, the frequency of such models decreases in the data.

Conclusion of The Univariate Exploration:¶

Visualizing mpg via histogram showed fewer models have higher mpg. Building a Pareto chart for the cylinders feature revealed that most models have 4-cylinder engines. The hp histogram is skewed to the right. As horsepower increases, the frequency decreases. As with horsepower, most models range between 50 and 150. Regarding time-to-60, most models take about 15 seconds to reach 60 miles per hour. Most cars in the data are US models according to the brand Pareto chart. These models were designed in the seventies and the eighties, as the year Pareto chart shows. The top five years about the number of brands are 1974, 1977, 1971, 1976, and 1980 or 1979. The cubicinches histogram is skewed to the right. Higher cubicinches involve lower frequency. The cubicinches feature mostly ranges between 100 and 350. The weightlbs histogram is skewed to the right. When the car's weight increases, the frequency decreases. Most models weigh about 1500 and 4500 pounds.

Bivariate Exploration¶

In this section, we'll investigate relationships between pairs of variables in our data.

1. Cubicinches Vs. Weights¶

In [19]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the cubicinches and weightlbs features:
sns.regplot(data=cars, x='cubicinches', y='weightlbs', x_jitter=0.8, scatter_kws={'alpha':0.5})
plt.xlabel('Cubicinches')
plt.ylabel('Weightlbs')
plt.title('Cubicinches Vs. Weights');

The scatterplot shows the positive correlation between cubicinches and weightlbs. Very intuitive and clear. Both the size of the car and its weight are positively correlated. The larger the car model, the heavier it gets.

2. Weights Vs. Miles Per Gallon¶

In [20]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the mpg and weightlbs features:
sns.regplot(data=cars, x='weightlbs', y='mpg', x_jitter=0.8, scatter_kws={'alpha':0.5})
plt.xlabel('Weightlbs')
plt.ylabel('MPG')
plt.title('Weights Vs. Miles Per Gallon');

The scatterplot shows the negative correlation between weightlbs and mpg. As we can see from this scatterplot, the heavier the car model, the fewer miles it travels per gallon, meaning it consumes much more fuel, which makes sense, right?! Logically, the same applies to the size of the car, given that the weight and the size of the car are positively correlated.

3. Horsepower Vs. Time-To-60¶

In [21]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the hp and time-to-60 features:
sns.regplot(data=cars, x='hp', y='time-to-60', x_jitter=0.8, scatter_kws={'alpha':0.5})
plt.xlabel('HP')
plt.ylabel('Time To 60')
plt.title('Horsepower Vs. Time-To-60');

The scatterplot shows the negative correlation between hp and time-to-60. The scatterplot makes perfect sense. The higher the horsepower of a car, the less time it takes to reach 60 miles per hour, meaning that it has higher acceleration and thus is faster.

4. Horsepower Vs. Miles Per Gallon¶

In [22]:
# Plotting a scatter plot of the mpg and hp features:
sns.regplot(data=cars, x='hp', y='mpg', x_jitter=0.8, scatter_kws={'alpha':0.5})
plt.xlabel('HP')
plt.ylabel('MPG')
plt.title('Horsepower Vs. Miles Per Gallon');

The scatterplot shows the negative correlation between hp and mpg. What a twist! Having a car with high horsepower doesn't mean high fuel efficiency. The higher the horsepower of a car engine, the fewer miles it travels per gallon. Stronger engines consume more fuel.

5. Brand Vs. Miles Per Gallon¶

In [23]:
# Plotting a violin plot of the brand and mpg features:
sns.violinplot(data=cars, x='brand', y='mpg', inner='quartile')
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('MPG')
plt.title('Brand Vs. Miles Per Gallon');
In [24]:
# Plotting a bar chart of the average mpg and brand features:
sns.barplot(data=cars, x='brand', y='mpg')
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('Average MPG')
plt.title('Brand VS. Average MPG');

According to the previous violin plot, we can clearly see, the Japanese brands have the highest median fuel efficiency, and the US brands have the lowest mpg median. The bar plots shows the average mpg for each brand. Japan brands have the highest mpg on average, while the US brands have the lowest mpg on average. European brands average mpg is much closer to the Japan brands mpg.

6. Brand Vs. Cubicinches¶

In [25]:
# Plotting a box plot of the brand and cubicinches features:
sns.boxplot(data=cars, x='brand', y='cubicinches')
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('Cubicinches')
plt.title('Brand Vs. Cubicinches');
In [26]:
# Plotting a bar chart of the average cubicinches and brand features:
sns.barplot(data=cars, x='brand', y='cubicinches')
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('Average Cubicinches')
plt.title('Brand VS. Average Cubincinches');

The US brands tend to have a larger size than the European and Japanese brands on average and hence heavier, as we proved earlier. That's why the US brands travel fewer miles per gallon. Less fuel efficiency.

7. Brand Vs. Time-To-60¶

In [27]:
# Plotting a box plot of the brand and time-to-60 features:
sns.boxplot(data=cars, x='brand', y='time-to-60')
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('Time To 60')
plt.title('Brand Vs. Time-To-60');
In [28]:
# Plotting a bar chart of the average time-to-60 and brand features:
sns.barplot(data=cars, x='brand', y='time-to-60')
plt.xlabel('Brand')
plt.ylabel('Average Time-To-60')
plt.title('Brand VS. Average Time-To-60');

As we can see, the US brands tend to have less time to reach their speed of 60 miles per hour than the European and Japanese brands on average and hence have more acceleration and speed. Based on a previous scatterplot, The US brands tend to have highest horsepower than the other brands as hp and time-to-60 are negatively correlated.

8. Year Vs. Miles Per Gallon¶

In [29]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the mpg and year features:
sns.regplot(data=cars, x='year', y='mpg', x_jitter=0.8, scatter_kws={'alpha':0.5})
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('MPG')
plt.title('Year Vs. Miles Per Gallon');
In [30]:
# Plotting a bar chart of the average mpg and year features:
sns.barplot(data=cars, x='year', y='mpg')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Average MPG')
plt.title('Year VS. Average MPG');
In [31]:
# Grouping the average mpg by year.
avg_mpg = cars.groupby('year')['mpg'].mean()
# Reseting the dataframe index.
avg_mpg = avg_mpg.reset_index()
In [32]:
# Plotting a line plot of the year and mpg features.
avg_mpg.plot('year', 'mpg', linewidth=2, legend=False)
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Average MPG')
plt.title('Average MPG By Year');

All the previous plots: the scatterplot, the bar chart, and the line plot, all show the positive correlation between year and mpg. Overtime, the car models in the data were improved regarding fuel consumption and have higher fuel efficiency. Maybe due to environmental awareness and competition between brands in reducing fuel costs and carbon dioxide emissions.

Conclusion of The Bivariate Exploration:¶

First, the cubicinches and weightlbs are positively correlated. The larger the car model, the heavier it becomes. The weightlbs and mpg are negatively correlated. The heavier the car model, the fewer miles it travels per gallon, thus it consumes more fuel. The hp and time-to-60 are negatively correlated, meaning that the higher the horsepower of a car, the less time it takes to reach 60 miles per hour. The hp and mpg are negatively correlated, meaning that the higher the horsepower of a car engine, the fewer miles it travels per gallon. On average the Japanese brands have the highest fuel efficiency than the European and US brands that have lower mpg. On average, the US brands tend to have a larger size than the European and Japanese brands. On average the US brands tend to have less time to reach their speed of 60 miles per hour than the European and Japanese brands. Lastly looking at how variables change overtime, the mpg and year features are positively correlated, meaning that recently designed models have higher mpg and thus burn less fuel. The correlation is also positive between time-to-60 and year, meaning with time, cars have less accelaration, which takes more time to reach the speed of 60 miles per hour. The correlation is negative between year and the following variables: cylinders, weightlbs (and cubicinches for that matter, since these two variables are positively correlated.), hp, which means recent cars have engines with less number of cylinders, these cars are relatively lighter and hence smaller, and lastly, their engines is less stronger with lower horsepower.

Multivariate Exploration¶

In this section, we'll create plots of three or more variables to investigate our data even further.

1. Cubicinches Vs. Weights By Brand¶

In [49]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the cubicinches and weightlbs features with color encodings for the brand feature:
g = sns.FacetGrid(data=cars, hue='brand', height=4, aspect=1.5, palette='magma_r')
g.map(sns.regplot, 'cubicinches', 'weightlbs', fit_reg=False, x_jitter=0.5)
g.add_legend(title='Brand')
plt.xlabel('Cubicinches')
plt.ylabel('Weightlbs')
plt.title('Cubicinches Vs. Weights By Brand');

The result is the same as the previous conclusions. The US brands are the largest and heaviest than the European and Japanese brands. The US models outnumber the Japanese and the European models in frequency.

2. Weights Vs. Miles Per Gallon By Brand¶

In [50]:
# Plotting a facet grid of the weightlbs & mpg scatterplots across the brand feature:
g = sns.FacetGrid(data=cars, col='brand', height=4)
g.map(sns.regplot, 'weightlbs', 'mpg', fit_reg=False, x_jitter=0.3)
# Adjusting title and axis labels directly.
g.fig.suptitle('Weights Vs. Miles Per Gallon By Brand', fontsize=12, va='bottom')
g.set_axis_labels(x_var='Weightlbs', y_var='MPG');

This facet grid reconfirms what we concluded from the bivariate visualizations. On average, the US brands have the highest weights and the lowest mpg (fuel efficiency). The Japanese and the European brands have higher MPG and lower weights. Also, the US models are much more frequent in the dataset than the other two brands, and the correlation is negative between the car's fuel efficiency and its weight in pounds.

3. Horsepower Vs. Time-To-60 By Brand¶

In [51]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the hp and time-to-60 features with color encodings for the brand feature:
g = sns.FacetGrid(data=cars, hue='brand', height=4, aspect=1.5, palette='mako_r')
g.map(sns.regplot, 'hp', 'time-to-60', fit_reg=False, x_jitter=0.5)
g.add_legend(title='Brand')
plt.xlabel('Horsepower')
plt.ylabel('Time To 60')
plt.title('Horsepower Vs. Time-To-60 By Brand');

The result is still the same as the previous conclusions. The US brands have higher horsepower and therefore less time to 60 than the European and Japanese brands. That is why the US brands are faster and thus burn more fuel. The US brands are much more frequent than others, and also the correlation between these two variables is negative.

4. Horsepower Vs. Miles Per Gallon By Brand¶

In [52]:
# Plotting a facet grid of the hp & mpg scatterplots across the brand feature:
g = sns.FacetGrid(data=cars, col='brand', height=4)
g.map(sns.regplot, 'hp', 'mpg', fit_reg=False, x_jitter=0.3)
# Adjusting title and axis labels directly.
g.fig.suptitle('Horsepower Vs. Miles Per Gallon By Brand', fontsize=12, va='bottom')
g.set_axis_labels(x_var='HP', y_var='MPG');

The facet grid reconfirms what we concluded from the previous bivariate visualizations. On average, the US brands have higher horsepower but lower mpg (fuel efficiency). The Japanese and the European brands have higher mpg but lower horsepower. Again, the US brands are much more frequent in the data than the Japanese and the European brands, and the correlation is negative between these two variables.

5. Year Vs. Miles Per Gallon By Brand¶

In [53]:
# Plotting a scatterplot of the year and mpg features with color encodings for the brand feature:
g = sns.FacetGrid(data=cars, hue='brand', height=4, aspect=1.5, palette='viridis_r')
g.map(sns.regplot, 'year', 'mpg', fit_reg=False, x_jitter=0.5)
g.add_legend(title='Brand')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('MPG')
plt.title('Year Vs. Miles Per Gallon By Brand');

The scatterplot shows a gradual increase in fuel efficiency of the new models over time for the three different brands, which indicates the importance of the fuel efficiency aspect of a car. Also, the US brands have lower mpg than the Japanese and European brands and are much more frequent, and the correlation between fuel consumption and year is positive.

Conclusion of The Multivariate Exploration:¶

In this section, I wanted to understand more about the brand feature, so I used non-positional encodings and faceting to visualize this feature. I plotted every scatterplot again with color encodings for the brand feature. The multivariate plots reconfirmed the insights we learned from the univariate and bivariate visualizations. The cubicinches and weightlbs are positively correlated. The US brands are the largest and heaviest than the European and Japanese brands. The weightlbs and mpg are negatively correlated. On average, the US brands have the highest weights and the lowest MPG (fuel efficiency), but the Japanese and the European brands have higher MPG and lower weights. The hp and time-to-60 are negatively correlated. The US brands have higher horsepower and therefore less time-to-60 (more acceleration) than the European and Japanese brands. The year and mpg are positively correlated. With time, the car models in the data were improved regarding fuel consumption and have higher MPG. Maybe due to environmental awareness or competition between brands in reducing fuel costs and carbon dioxide emissions.
